Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: Twelve identical workers can set up one stage in two hours. Fourteen such workers can set up the seating in four hours. How many workers are needed to set up one stage and the seating in eight hours?
at: Twelve identical workers can set up

slides.say: Identical workers, in a group, so it's a team question. They ask for the number of workers.
at: They ask for the number of workers

slides.say: But careful, there are two jobs. One team sets up the stage, and another team sets up the seating. Both teams work at the same time, during the same eight hours.

We'll solve it in three different ways. Let's start with the math way, with the V method. First the stage. Row one is twelve workers, one stage, two hours. Row two is the question mark, one stage, eight hours.
at: Row two is the question mark

slides.say: The question mark is in the team. So the V joins twelve, one and two. We multiply them, and divide by the other two, one and eight.
at: and divide by the other two

slides.say: Twelve times one times two is twenty-four. Twenty-four divided by eight is three workers.
Now the seating. Fourteen workers, one seating, four hours. And the question mark, one seating, eight hours.
The V joins fourteen, one and four. Fourteen times one times four is fifty-six. Fifty-six divided by eight is seven workers.
Three workers on the stage, and seven on the seating, at the same time. Three plus seven is ten workers.
Careful with twenty-six, choice number one. That's twelve plus fourteen, the workers from the givens. But with eight hours, we need fewer workers.
So ten workers. That's choice number two.
[pause] Now by understanding, with ratios. We start again from the givens. Like in the lesson, here only one thing changes, the time. The job stays the same. So ratios are quick.
The stage took two hours, and now we have eight. Two to eight is times four.
at: Two to eight is times four

slides.say: More time means fewer workers. That's the opposite way, so we divide the workers by four. Twelve divided by four is three.
The seating took four hours, and now we have eight. That's times two.
So half the workers. Fourteen divided by two is seven. And we send the rest home.
Three plus seven is ten workers again.
at: Three plus seven is ten workers again

slides.say: [pause] And the math way with worker-hours, like in the lesson. We start again from the givens. Think of the boss who pays by the hour.
The stage takes twelve workers for two hours. Twelve times two is twenty-four worker-hours.
The seating takes fourteen workers for four hours. Fourteen times four is fifty-six worker-hours.
Both jobs together need twenty-four plus fifty-six, eighty worker-hours.
We have eight hours. So we need eighty divided by eight, ten workers.
Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number two is our answer
